Our results establish low-noise switching as a promising approach to broadband quantum memories combining high transmission, encoding versatility, and programmable temporal-mode control.
item.dc:creator: Domenico Compagnini, Noemi Tagliavacche, Sara Congia, Andrea Bernardi, Marco Liscidini, Matteo Galli, Daniele Bajoni

item.title: Graph-Spectral Entanglement
item.description: arXiv:2606.31453v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a unified graph-spectral framework for quantifying multipartite entanglement, built upon an entanglement graph and its associated entanglement matrix. The framework accommodates general subsystem and partition structures of composite quantum systems, while offering a complementary geometric and network perspective on characterizing multipartite quantum correlations. We prove that the resulting graph-spectral entanglement satisfies the requirements of an entanglement measure. Furthermore, we derive a multipartite monogamy relation and, based on the resulting spectral hierarchy, introduce residual graph-spectral entanglement for arbitrary multipartite states. This establishes a general construction of residual entanglement beyond conventional qubit-based formulations and provides a new approach to investigating, quantifying, witnessing, and classifying multipartite entanglement in both theoretical and experimental settings.
item.dc:creator: Vahid Azimi-Mousolou

item.title: Multi-stage Quantum Amplifier Readout Chain
item.description: arXiv:2607.07614v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-stage cryogenic readout chains with a wide bandwidth and added noise within a few quanta of the quantum limit are frequently constructed using traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (TWPAs) as the first stage, and a semiconductor amplifier as the second stage. Unfortunately, for highly-scaled superconducting detector arrays, or quantum information systems, and space-based observatories, the power dissipation of the semiconductor amplifier becomes problematic from the perspective of available cryogenic cooling power near 3 K. Here we demonstrate a readout chain based on a two-stage kinetic inductance TWPA (KTWPA). This quantum-amplifier-based-readout-chain (QARC) provides sufficient gain that a cryogenic semiconductor follow-on amplifier can be eliminated without degradation of the system noise. Due to the ultra-low dissipation of KTWPAs and their higher output-power-to-total-power ratio, the QARC dissipates approximately three orders of magnitude less power than readout chains containing semiconductor amplifiers while adding noise of less than 2 quanta over a 1 GHz bandwidth. In addition, by leveraging the high power handling of kinetic inductance technology, the QARC maintains an input compression point of -93 dBm, which exceeds that of many contemporary Josephson-junction-based parametric amplifiers.
item.dc:creator: Logan Howe, Andrea Giachero, Michael Vissers, Corwin Shiu, Shannon Duff, Jason Austermann, Johannes Hubmayr, Joel Ullom

item.title: Absolute displacement calibration of a levitated nanoparticle with real-time heterodyne demodulation
item.description: arXiv:2607.09912v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We report a heterodyne scheme for the position readout of an optomechanical system, in particular an optically levitated nanoparticle, based on digital in-phase and quadrature demodulation on a field-programmable gate array. Compared to the standard homodyne approach, it offers three key advantages: it requires no phase lock, it produces a signal linearly proportional to the particle displacement, and its calibration is immune to drifts in the optical power of the local oscillator and of the scattered field. Combined with a vectorial model of the focal field, it measures the displacement in length units without free parameters. Through simultaneous homodyne and heterodyne measurements on the same trapped particle we demonstrate these advantages: the heterodyne follows a driven particle linearly up to amplitudes at which the homodyne response folds back, and calibrates the homodyne, whose standard thermometric calibration we find biased by 33 %. Inverting equipartition, the calibrated readout measures the mass of the particle with an uncertainty below 1 %, after removing a bias of up to 20 % caused by absorption heating at 1550 nm. The method can be used in any optomechanical system based on phase readout.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Tandeitnik, Gabriel Dias, Thiago Guerreiro

item.title: Filon Methods for Highly Oscillatory Controlled Quantum Systems
item.description: arXiv:2607.13580v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fast and accurate classical simulation of quantum systems is a central challenge in the design and control of quantum computers, but the highly oscillatory dynamics of these systems severely limit the efficiency of standard numerical methods. To address this, we adapt Filon quadrature for oscillatory integrals into two numerical methods, called Filon and Controlled Filon, for solving linear systems of ODEs with highly oscillatory solutions. We tailor both methods for efficient implementation in controlled quantum systems, and the Controlled Filon method additionally accounts for the oscillatory structure of the control pulses. We show by numerical experiments that these methods significantly reduce the computational cost of accurately simulating systems of superconducting transmon qubits by decreasing the number of timesteps needed to reach a given level of precision, with only a modest increase in the cost per timestep. For a realistic simulation of the dynamics of a CNOT gate, the Controlled Filon method is the most efficient method tested at every target accuracy, outperforming the best Hermite method by up to 6x and the Hermite method of the same order by up to 500x.
item.dc:creator: Spencer Lee, Daniel Appel\"o

item.title: No Finite NPA Level Characterizes the Complete Quantum Set in the Simplest Bell Scenario
item.description: arXiv:2607.14569v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Navascu\'es--Pironio--Ac\'in (NPA) hierarchy provides increasingly tighter semidefinite outer approximations to the set of quantum correlations, while its dual programs give sum-of-squares certificates that can establish exact quantum bounds for Bell inequalities and yield self-testing relations. We show that no finite level of the NPA hierarchy can exactly characterize the set of quantum correlations, even in the simplest Bell scenario. For the symmetric doubly tilted CHSH inequality, the maximal quantum violation vanishes cubically as the tilting parameter approaches its critical value, while the error of every fixed NPA level relative to this violation diverges. We construct a family of two-qubit strategies for which the gap between the exact quantum bound and the attained Bell value, divided by the quantum violation, tends to the Motzkin polynomial in rescaled measurement angles. If the relative error remained bounded, the fixed-level NPA certificates would yield a sum-of-squares representation of this limiting polynomial plus a nonnegative constant, which is impossible.
item.dc:creator: Anubhav Chaturvedi

item.title: Optimal Quantum Metrology for Probing the Unruh Effect with Uniformly Accelerated Two-Level Atoms
item.description: arXiv:2607.16701v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a quantum metrological framework for optimizing the probing of the Unruh effect using uniformly accelerated two-level atomic probes. The acceleration-dependent factor generated during the atom--field interaction is encoded in the atomic state and can be estimated through repeated quantum measurements. For a fixed total probe time, which characterizes the available measurement resource, we optimize the interrogation time of individual probes, the initial atomic state, and the corresponding measurement basis to minimize the estimation uncertainty. We show that the achievable precision is governed by the Fisher information accumulated per unit probe time. Under a fixed total probe time, shorter evolution times of individual probes allow for more sequential measurements, leading to a significant improvement in the estimation precision. The optimal initial state depends on both the acceleration factor and the probe evolution time. In particular, the excited state provides superior sensitivity in the weak-acceleration and small probe time regime. Furthermore, we determine the minimum total probe time required to resolve the acceleration-dependent signal associated with the Unruh effect and demonstrate that this requirement can be substantially reduced by employing atomic systems with larger transition dipole moments. Our results establish an optimized quantum metrological strategy for probing acceleration-induced quantum effects and provide a systematic approach toward the experimental investigation of the Unruh effect.
item.dc:creator: Yao Jin

item.title: High-purity entanglement mediated by magnons despite weak coupling
item.description: arXiv:2607.19533v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Entangling distant spins via a shared magnonic bus typically faces a tradeoff: stronger spin-magnon coupling increases the entanglement fidelity, but also the spin decay rate. We propose a protocol that breaks this tradeoff. The magnons couple only to a transition outside the computational basis, in which the Bell state is created. Our protocol is probabilistic, and weak coupling reduces the success probability but not the fidelity. We analyze a setup where the spins are two nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers near a magnetic wire. In the absence of NV dephasing, the protocol reaches unit fidelity with a maximally entangled state, for arbitrarily weak coupling. In our simulations via the Monte-Carlo wavefunction approach, the NV-magnon coupling is taken to be one-third of the magnon linewidth. Considering finite NV dephasing, we predict a fidelity of >0.99 for a state-of-the-art rate, and an optimal fidelity of 0.91 for a moderate rate, both at 0.6% success probability.
item.dc:creator: Sanchar Sharma

item.title: Effect-valued measurement models and contextuality
item.description: arXiv:2607.25900v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We generalize the Abramsky--Brandenburger sheaf-theoretic treatment of contextuality by replacing probability distributions with distributions valued in a convex effect algebra \(A\). This yields a notion of \(A\)-valued measurement model encompassing probabilistic, deterministic, and quantum measurement structures within a single framework. States \(\sigma:A\to[0,1]\) induce ordinary empirical models, allowing observable behaviour to be viewed as arising from effect-valued measurement data. This leads to a distinction between internal contextuality of \(A\)-models and observable contextuality after state evaluation. We analyze the relationship between these notions and identify coherence conditions under which observable classical explanations assemble into internal ones. Using the ordered-vector-space representation of effect modules, we show that non-contextuality is characterized by feasibility of an associated cone program, generalizing the linear-programming formulation of contextuality in the probabilistic case. We also introduce an effect-valued contextual fraction and study its relation to observable contextuality witnesses. We show how cone duality leads to a notion of Bell witnesses for contextuality as a direct generalization of Bell inequalities. Finally, we analyze sharp realizability and uniform dilation for measurement models, clarifying the relationship between general POVMs and projective measurements, and show how resource-indexed effect structures induce graded monads generalizing the quantum monad.
item.dc:creator: Samson Abramsky, Lucas Stinchcombe

item.title: Two-photon interference from as-grown InAsP/InP quantum dots under detuned excitation
item.description: arXiv:2607.26957v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this study, we investigate as-grown InAsP/InP quantum dots emitting in the third telecommunication window. The investigated quantum dots are embedded directly in an aluminium-free InP matrix without additional barrier material. A large excitation-emission detuning of 32 meV enables efficient suppression of scattered laser light while retaining several advantages of near-resonant excitation. The single-photon nature of the emission is confirmed by a Hanbury Brown and Twiss experiment, yielding a raw second-order autocorrelation value of $g_{\mathrm{raw}}^{(2)}(0)=0.076(6)$. A Hong-Ou-Mandel measurement is used to determine the degree of indistinguishability of single photons and reveals as-measured visibilities of $V=0.038(8)$ and $V=0.108(18)$ for excitation pulse separations of 13.1 ns and 5.3 ns, respectively. We observe finite photon indistinguishability in as-grown InAsP/InP quantum dots under detuned quasi-resonant excitation, without deliberate Purcell enhancement.
item.dc:creator: Maja Wasiluk, Anna Musia{\l}, Pawe{\l} Mrowi\'nski, Johann Peter Reithmaier, Mohamed Benyoucef, Wojciech Rudno-Rudzi\'nski

item.title: Embedded quantum computing for many-body surface reaction
item.description: arXiv:2607.27009v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predictive simulations of catalytic interfaces require correlated electronic-structure treatments that describe localized chemical transformations while retaining the influence of the extended metallic environment. We introduce QC-DFET, a quantum-computing density-functional embedding framework that maps surface-reaction active spaces to compact, environment-aware qubit Hamiltonians. A reaction-consistent active-space protocol preserves orbital continuity along reaction coordinates, while quantum-selected configuration interaction based on measurements from the Zuchongzhi superconducting quantum processor and strongly contracted perturbation theory capture static and dynamic correlation. On Cu(111), QC-DFET treats active spaces up to 28 qubits and is validated through a hierarchy of experimentally constrained surface-chemistry challenges. H2 dissociation/desorption tests balanced bond breaking and recombination barriers, CO adsorption tests site selectivity and metal-adsorbate bonding, and formate hydrogenation tests competing hydrogenation branches with different kinetic and thermodynamic signatures. Across these cases, QC-DFET reproduces bidirectional H2 barriers, recovers the observed top-site preference and adsorption strength of CO, and reconciles the experimentally benchmarked H2COO* reverse barrier with the lower forward barrier to HCOOH*. These results establish embedded quantum computing as a practical route to correlated surface-reaction energetics.
item.dc:creator: Dedong Wan, Xiaopeng Li, Yi Fan, Jie Liu, Xiongzhi Zeng, Zhenyu Li

item.title: Finite size scaling of bitstring probability distributions for Rydberg arrays
item.description: arXiv:2607.27013v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We calculate the probabilities $p_{\{n\}}$ of the measured bitstrings $\{n\}$ for the vacuum of Rydberg ladders with $N_q$ atoms. As $N_q$ increases, the $p_{\{n\}}$ decrease but become more dense in the low $p$ region, raising the possibility that their smallness could be compensated by their large number. The importance of the low probability states can be estimated from the cumulative probability distribution $\Sigma(p_{\Lambda},N_q)$, which is the probability to observe any state having a probability $p\leq p_{\Lambda}$. For not too large values of $p_{\Lambda}$, it is possible to approximately collapse the $\Sigma(p_{\Lambda},N_q)$ for successive $N_q$ into a function that resembles the Fermi function when plotted as a function of $-\ln(p_{\Lambda})$. We show that the number of shots necessary to reduce $\Sigma(p_{\Lambda},N_q)$ to a sufficiently low value grows exponentially with $N_q$. We discuss the implications for calculating observables associated with the vacuum. We show how the accuracy of these observables may or may not be robust against the number of shots. The collapsed probabilities occur in other systems, where they typically are on one side of the phase transition, in a basis dependent way.
item.dc:creator: Zane Ozzello, Avi Kaufman, Yannick Meurice

item.title: SWAP Gate Between Polarization and Time-Bin Qubits on a Single Photon
item.description: arXiv:2607.27144v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-degree-of-freedom photonic quantum processing requires coherent routing between qubit encodings on a single photon. We propose a SWAP circuit between polarization and time-bin qubits using polarization-dependent delays and synchronized electro-optic modulation, analyzing phase-calibration, voltage-accuracy, and timing requirements for experimental realization. The architecture follows a three-CNOT SWAP decomposition, using two polarization beam splitter (PBS)--delay--PBS stages to produce polarization-controlled time-bin parity flips. Between these stages, an electro-optic modulator (EOM) driven by a voltage waveform synchronized to a time-bin grid flips polarization in odd bins while leaving even bins unchanged. A final PBS--delay--PBS compensation stage delays the $H$-polarized components by $2\Delta t$, aligning the relevant $H$ and $V$ amplitudes in common output time bins. We describe an infinite grid of repeating early/late time-bin pairs, labelling early bins as even ($\ket{E}$) and late bins as odd ($\ket{O}$). Throughout, we use these even/odd labels without explicit pair indices. A delay of one bin spacing $\Delta t$ moves an even bin to the following odd bin and an odd bin to the following even bin, corresponding to the early slot of the next pair in a traditional early/late encoding. Tracking the polarization and time-bin states through the complete circuit, we establish the resulting SWAP transformation. We identify the optical phase conditions required for coherent operation and discuss their calibration and compensation. We also quantify the effect of EOM voltage errors on polarization-flip probability and present an illustrative timing budget based on switching, detector resolution, and timing jitter.
item.dc:creator: Adam Sultan, Connor Kupchak

item.title: Quantum fluctuation relations in first-detection processes
item.description: arXiv:2608.06194v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We derive three quantum fluctuation relations for systems undergoing repeated projective measurements. These fluctuation relations characterize the work that can be extracted from a quantum device when a first-detection event triggers a mechanical operation leading to positive work production. The correction to the standard quantum Jarzynski equality depends logarithmically on the mean first-detection time for the time-reversed dynamics. Application of Jensen's inequality leads to fundamental limits on both the total work involved in the repeated measurements and final mechanical operation, and the extracted work alone. An analogous inequality is derived for the work performed exclusively during the sequence of repeated projective measurements. The general case of a device connected to an external environment is also considered.
item.dc:creator: A. Imparato

item.title: Controlled dynamics of a multi-component discrete-time quantum walker
item.description: arXiv:2608.13161v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate a discrete-time quantum walk of a three-component quantum particle on a one-dimensional lattice. As coin operators, we employ parameterized rotations generated by the Gell-Mann matrices, which enable systematic tuning of the couplings between the internal components. We analyze how these couplings influence and control the dynamics by systematically exploring the position-space probability distribution across a broad region of the parameter space. To quantify the impact of different inter-component couplings, we further examine the ratio of the mean position to the variance in each half of the lattice. Our results indicates that the system supports a rich variety of transport regimes, ranging from nearly symmetric, rapidly spreading walks to strongly anisotropic dynamics with partial localization. This framework thus provides a new avenue for engineering targeted spreading and trapping behavior in multicomponent discrete-time quantum walks.
item.dc:creator: Vikash Mittal, Tomasz Sowi\'nski

item.title: The form of dissipation shapes what a quantum reservoir remembers
item.description: arXiv:2608.14181v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dissipation sets how long a quantum reservoir computer remembers its past inputs, and its rate is the usual control. Here we show that its form matters as much, for how a memory is stored, written and read. When the qubits decay independently, stronger loss shortens the memory. When they decay collectively, the quantum Zeno effect holds the system in dark states that do not decay, and stronger loss prolongs the memory. A longer memory is harder to write, because it leaves more time for new inputs to mix with the inputs already stored. We prove that the number of inputs mixed into a stored signal is, on average, the memory lifetime times the fraction of the signal that one input mixes. We also prove that this number stays fixed, however long the memory lasts, when the input amplitude falls as the inverse square root of the lifetime. A weaker input leaves a fainter signal to read out, so the form of the dissipation, the input amplitude and the measurement budget have to be chosen together.
item.dc:creator: Markus Baumann, Itamar Fink, Johannes Wittmann, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien, Jonas Stein

item.title: Anti-Zeno boost in an autonomous quantized-piston thermal machine
item.description: arXiv:2608.15899v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Anti-Zeno enhancement of quantum heat machines has been established for working fluids driven by an external classical field, but whether it can enhance extractable-work accumulation in an autonomously evolving quantized piston remains an important question. Here we study an autonomous thermal machine in which a two-level working fluid is coupled to a quantized harmonic piston and to two spectrally separated reservoirs, without external modulation. We derive a finite-time master equation for the resulting carrier and sideband channels, whose rates interpolate between the Zeno, anti-Zeno, and Markovian regimes as the coupling time is varied. For an initially coherent piston, the machine charges the piston and generates more ergotropy than the Markovian reference in the anti-Zeno window. Reversing the same retained channels turns the device into a finite-resource refrigerator with enhanced cooling. The anti-Zeno effect therefore increases the rate of operation while leaving the underlying carrier and sideband energy ratios unchanged. These channel ratios remain consistent with the usual Carnot bounds over the operating regimes considered here. Our results establish finite-time reservoir sampling as a mechanism for enhancing autonomous thermal-machine operation with a quantized piston.
item.dc:creator: M. Tahir Naseem

item.title: Dissipative framework for subsystem dynamics of noninteracting quantum chains
item.description: arXiv:2608.21336v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When only local observables of a many-body quantum system are of interest, it is desirable to formulate a reduced description within the Hilbert space of the corresponding subsystem, with the remaining degrees of freedom traced out and acting as an environment. Assuming initially uncorrelated states and Gaussian environments, we develop a framework for reconstructing the local dynamical generator of noninteracting quantum chains, with polynomial computational effort. As an application, we consider two representative models: a bipartitioned Kitaev chain and a Kitaev chain boundary-coupled to a fully connected free-fermion environment. In both models, strong subsystem-environment coupling leads to non-Markovian dynamics characterized by ballistic spreading of the Lindblad dissipator support within the subsystem. On the other hand, weak coupling to a fully connected environment yields predominantly boundary-localized, Markovian dissipation. Our work highlights the implications of subsystem-environment correlations on the generator of local dynamics, beyond the conventional weak-coupling approximations.
item.dc:creator: Michele Coppola, Mari Carmen Ba\~nuls, Zala Lenar\v{c}i\v{c}

item.title: Collective photon echoes in the Tavis-Cummings model: distribution independence, two detuning regimes, and the Dicke ladder
item.description: arXiv:2608.21442v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An ensemble of $N$ two-level molecules prepared in its ground state and sharing a lossless cavity with a weak field does not simply absorb: the intensity collapses and then recurs, in a train of collective photon echoes. Working from the exact solution of the Tavis-Cummings model in the few-photon regime $\bar n<N$, we confirm the echo time $\tau_E=4\pi\sqrt{N+\Delta}/g$ at resonance from $N=5$ to $N=400$, and separate it from the alternative $4\pi\sqrt{N-\bar n+\Delta}/g$ by a direct test: the recurrence period is independent of $\bar n$ to $0.8\%$ across a factor of six in $\bar n$, where the alternative predicts shifts of up to $17\%$. The initial state, the ground state, requires no preparation. The echo time is independent of the initial photon distribution - coherent, thermal, squeezed and oscillatory-squeezed distributions with variances from 2 to 34 all recur together - but the echo amplitude is not: it varies at the tens-of-percent level at fixed mean, including a factor of 1.8 with the squeezing phase. Detuning organizes the dynamics into two clean regimes separated by a fragmented crossover; the echo time in the dispersive branch is exactly one-half that of the resonant branch, a factor derived from second-order dispersive perturbation theory with leading correction $5Ng^2/\delta^2$, and sufficient detuning removes the dependence on the initial Dicke state. For arbitrary initial $|r=N/2,m\rangle$, emission replaces absorption at $m\simeq-N/2+\bar n$, and the echo envelope acquires one component per step up the ladder. Lindblad simulations with all loss channels acting simultaneously, and full-Hilbert-space disorder simulations, show the first echoes to be observable at $N\sim5$-$20$ on an existing five-qubit superconducting device: the echo survives cavity decay with contrast $\sim e^{-\kappa\tau_E/2}$, photons being shielded while resident in the emitters.
item.dc:creator: Michael Tavis

item.title: Reading Convivial Solipsism: Towards a Logic of Perspectival Facts
item.description: arXiv:2608.26361v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Convivial Solipsism is easily misunderstood. Because it denies the absoluteness of observed events while preserving the universality of quantum mechanics, it invites objections that are often formulated in a classical, non-perspectival language. Some objections arise from importing assumptions that Convivial Solipsism rejects; others challenge whether those rejections yield an adequate account of observers, communication, and scientific practice. This article distinguishes these two kinds of criticism. In particular, it reconstructs a family of objections that arise in discussions of Convivial Solipsism, especially in connection with Wigner's friend and extended Wigner's friend scenarios. The objections are useful because they identify the conceptual discipline required by any interpretation that takes non-absolute facts seriously. The central claim is that observational facts must be indexed to perspectives. The mistake consists in removing these indices and then treating the resulting expressions as if they belonged to a single global factual domain. This leads to apparent contradictions and to false dilemmas concerning consciousness, communication, other minds, and intersubjectivity. When that is taken into account, it appears that Convivial Solipsism is a discipline of perspectival discourse. The paper also develops an analogy between two restrictions on global descriptions. Quantum contextuality prevents certain families of measurement statistics from being represented within a single noncontextual Kolmogorovian probability model. Likewise, Convivial Solipsism requires a perspectival logic governing the formation and combination of observational statements, while retaining classical reasoning for well-formed indexed propositions. A detailed formalization of the perspectival logic outlined here will be provided in a forthcoming paper.
item.dc:creator: Herve Zwirn

item.title: From Quantum Cryptography to Intuitionism and beyond: relativity, many-worlds and non-locality
item.description: arXiv:2609.07127v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: After a recollection of some of my encounters with Gilles Brassard, on the occasion of his 70th birthday I present, first, a new idea on creation of new information at a limited rate. Next, I develop the idea that "indeterminacy is relative" [Entropy {23} 1326 (2021)] and how this illuminates the compatibility between relativity and non-locality.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Gisin

item.title: Bottom-Up Design of Quantum Optical Experiments Using Discrete Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2609.08073v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Designing quantum optical experiments requires searching over discrete circuit topologies and continuous parameters, often leading to multiple possible realizations of the same target state. Graph-based methods commonly address this problem by optimizing a dense graph and pruning it toward a single circuit. We introduce \texttt{Grinch}, a bottom-up reward-driven generative framework that learns to sample optical graphs directly from fidelity-based rewards without relying on a pre-existing training dataset. We demonstrate the framework on multipartite entangled states, graph and cluster states, and nonlocal photonic-gate targets, obtaining multiple high-fidelity optical graphs. For nonlocal photonic gates, we obtain Toffoli constructions requiring two ancillas and alternative CNOT and Toffoli designs when connections between ancilla nodes are restricted. For state preparation, we identify asymptotic solutions for targets that cannot be generated exactly by graphs. Using the discovered topologies, we derive analytic families of optical experiments with explicit interference mechanisms and fidelity--rate relations, showing how generative design can support interpretable scientific discovery. These findings illustrate a reward-driven approach to quantum optical inverse design, exploring alternative circuit topologies while directly incorporating connectivity constraints into the search process.
item.dc:creator: Isaac L. Huidobro-Meezs, Sim\'on Paiva-Ortega, Rodrigo A. Vargas-Hern\'andez

item.title: Spectral Core-Tail Architecture for Locally Certified Gibbs-State Preparation
item.description: arXiv:2609.09291v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a constructive method for designing Gibbs-state preparation circuits near tractable reference models, together with an explicit local error analysis. The spectral core-tail architecture (SCTA) combines a tractable thermal core and a unitary tail, defining a core-frame residual that measures the Hamiltonian mismatch from the target. We derive a local Gibbs-state error bound from the residual using the Kubo-Mori response theory. This bound is volume uniform when the response meets a shell summability condition and the relevant local data remain uniform with system size. We present three anchor Hamiltonian classes that admit exact core-tail constructions with zero residuals. For small deformations around an exact anchor, we employ a Schrieffer-Wolff-type reduction procedure that updates the core and constructs a correction to the tail. We prove that, under locality and solvability assumptions, the first-order reduction leaves a residual whose strength is quadratic in the deformation strength, with bounds independent of system size. A formal recursion extends the construction to arbitrary perturbative order at fixed volume, conditional on order-by-order solvability. Finite-size numerical tests on deformed graph-stabilizer Hamiltonians verify the quadratic suppression of both the residual and the local Gibbs-state error in the perturbative regime. The correction generators also provide a useful variational ansatz beyond perturbative control.
item.dc:creator: Rui-Hao Li

item.title: High-fidelity conditional-squeezing gate in superconducting circuits via refocusing
item.description: arXiv:2609.10655v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a conditional-squeezing gate for superconducting circuits, which squeezes one or two modes of a resonator along a direction determined by the state of a dispersively coupled qubit. We show that the fidelity of this gate can be substantially improved by a refocusing protocol, in an architecture accessible with current technology whose key element is a SQUID-terminated resonator. The refocusing protocol relies on a symmetry of the Hamiltonian that is absent in the previously proposed controlled-squeezing gate, which squeezes the resonator only for one state of the control qubit and, ideally, acts trivially otherwise. We apply the refocused gate to encode an arbitrary qubit state into superpositions of single- and two-mode squeezed vacuum states, in which single-photon losses are detectable through parity measurements. Including nonlinearities and dissipation, the conditional gate consistently outperforms the controlled-squeezing gate, and, for optimistic but achievable experimental parameters, the encoding reaches fidelities above 0.99 for all qubit states.
item.dc:creator: Roman Schiaffino, Fernando C. Lombardo, Juan Pablo Paz

item.title: Universal Defect Statistics in Reverse Quenches
item.description: arXiv:2609.14960v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We extend the generalized Kibble-Zurek mechanism (gKZM) to reverse quench protocols using a stochastic description of defect formation finding that the mean defect density after a reverse quench equals twice the forward quench defect-number variance per unit volume. This relation, universally valid within the stochastic framework of the gKZM, makes the forward quench variance accessible through a reverse quench defect density measurement. We verify the equality analytically and numerically in the uniform one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model, and numerically in its bond-disordered variant, including a regime where defect scaling departs from a pure power-law in quench time. Our result also suggests an experimental route to probing quantum critical behavior: reverse quenches that begin and end in the paramagnetic phase may allow to reveal critical exponents using global magnetic-field control and magnetization measurements, without resolving individual defects.
item.dc:creator: Eduard J. Braun, Daniel Rubin, Margaux Cartier, Gerhard Z\"urn, Matthias Weidem\"uller

item.title: Feature-Adaptive Fusion in Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Networks for Robust Biomedical Image Classification
item.description: arXiv:2609.15267v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hybrid quantum--classical neural networks offer a promising framework for integrating quantum circuits into machine learning in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum era. However, fixed or globally shared fusion strategies used in many existing hybrid models may limit the effective integration of complementary classical and quantum information. To address this limitation, we propose a Feature-Adaptive Fusion Hybrid Quantum--Classical Neural Network (FAF-HQNN) for biomedical image classification. The proposed model combines a classical deep feature encoder with a variational quantum circuit (VQC) and employs a feature-adaptive fusion mechanism to dynamically weight classical and quantum predictions across samples and classes. Under the evaluated settings, FAF-HQNN achieves competitive accuracy on PathMNIST and BloodMNIST compared to internal variants and external hybrid quantum--classical baselines. On PathMNIST, FAF-HQNN achieves higher aggregate mean accuracy than all evaluated baselines under both Gaussian and Poisson noise. These results suggest that feature-adaptive fusion may help improve classification performance within the evaluated framework.
item.dc:creator: Yan-Yan Hou, Jian Li, Chongqiang Ye, Hengji Li, Zhuo Wang, Qinghui Liu

item.title: A complete classification of the existence of finite-dimensional quantum solutions to inconsistent linear constraint systems
item.description: arXiv:2609.16490v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Linear constraint systems (LCS) provide a compact algebraic language for nonlocal games and state-independent contextuality. In the binary case the Mermin--Peres square shows that inconsistent LCS can be solved by promoting variables to local Pauli operators, whereas a series of no-go results excludes analogous Pauli-, Clifford- and monomial unitary-based constructions at odd prime modulus. We first isolate the reason for this difference: for tensor-product quantum solutions, the obstruction to a classical solution of a LCS over $\mathbb{Z}_n$ decomposes into obstruction classes carried by the individual factors. As a consequence, a genuinely global obstruction cannot arise solely by tensoring locally unobstructed systems. The argument is specific to odd modulus; at even modulus the reordering phase need not vanish, as in Pauli-based examples. Given this distinction, we instead associate LCS to finite arrangements of rank-one projectors and resolutions of the identity in finite-dimensional vector spaces. Quantum solvability for such LCS is automatic and the search for a quantum-classical gap rests entirely on proving classical unsatisfiability of the underlying modular incidence problem of the arrangement. By relating such LCS with group-valued frame functions, we identify a family of examples in the work of [Harding, Jager, and Smith, Int. J. Theor. Phys. 44, 539 (2005)]. To establish the (non)existence of classically unsatisfiable LCS over $\mathbb{Z}_n$ with quantum solutions in all dimensions $d$ and for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, we further construct explicit examples for the cases $d=n$ prime. Our main result thus positively resolves the existence problem of such LCS beyond the binary case: such systems exist if and only if $d\geq 3$ and $\gcd(n,d)>1$. Moreover, we establish the existence of LCS with a quantum-classical gap over finite fields if and only if $d\geq 3$ and $p\mid d$.
item.dc:creator: Markus Frembs

item.title: Encrypted Quantum Cloning Beyond Maximal Entanglement: Exact Classification of Multipartite Resources
item.description: arXiv:2609.28241v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Encrypted quantum cloning distributes an unknown $k$-qubit state among $m$ individually concealed signals, each permitting exact recovery when combined with a common quantum key. While canonical constructions rely on maximally entangled resources, they do not establish which multipartite states are necessary or sufficient for this task. Here we derive necessary and sufficient conditions characterizing all pure resources compatible with a prescribed sector-wise two-Pauli encoder for $m\geq 2$, with necessity holding for arbitrary completely positive trace-preserving recovery maps. The classification reveals a sharp parity dependence: even $m$ requires maximal signal--key entanglement, whereas odd $m$ admits nonmaximally entangled resources when their residual signal correlations belong to an encoder-selected commuting algebra. Beyond this architecture, we show that exact recovery from every authorized subsystem under arbitrary unitary encoders acting on the input and signals while leaving the key untouched necessarily implies perfect individual concealment, requires at least $(m-1)k$ ebits of signal--key entanglement, and imposes spectral constraints on the resource. For graph states, the classification reduces to an exact cut-kernel criterion, enabling binary certification and constructive Clifford recovery. In particular, a rank-deficient three-output resource in the YZ/ZY branch attains the general entanglement lower bound with two ebits rather than three. We also exclude the entire Dicke family, including $W$ states, within the two-Pauli architecture. Together, these results distinguish fundamental entanglement requirements from encoder-dependent correlation constraints, providing an exact characterization of resource admissibility and a constructive recovery framework for graph states.
item.dc:creator: Pritam Roy, Shashank Gupta

item.title: A Three-Party W-State Quantum Secret Sharing Protocol with X-Gate Encoding and Forbidden-Outcome Detection
item.description: arXiv:2609.31472v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a new three-party quantum secret sharing (QSS) protocol based on a three-qubit W state for distributing a predetermined sequence of classical bits. Alice encodes each bit using X gates and randomly applies Hadamard gates to the transmitted qubits. Her Hadamard-gate choices and the measurement bases independently chosen by Bob and Charlie determine the type of each round (information, test or semi-information) during transmission, without designating test rounds in advance. Suitable semi-information rounds provide additional opportunities for secret transmission and improve efficiency. The protocol combines secret transmission and tests for forbidden outcomes within the same ensemble of encoded W states. In the ideal model without an attack, transmitting an n-bit secret requires an average of 3n protocol rounds, giving a qubit efficiency of 1/9. We analyze intercept-and-resend and entangle-and-measure attacks by an internal adversary and derive their single-round and cumulative detection probabilities. For the entangle-and-measure attack, we relate the information obtainable through an ancillary system to the probability of forbidden test outcomes. The protocol is implemented in Python using Qiskit and evaluated through ideal simulation and experiments on IBM Quantum hardware. The simulation results are consistent with the theoretical predictions, while hardware measurements characterize round efficiency, reconstruction errors, forbidden-outcome probabilities and the information obtained through the specified ancilla measurement. A calibrated statistical criterion accounts for forbidden outcomes caused by hardware noise, with detection and false-alarm probabilities evaluated using a binomial model with measured rates. This analysis connects the ideal protocol predictions with a finite-sample assessment under the specified attack models and statistical assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Timur R. Teregulov, Elena R. Loubenets

item.title: Nash Equilibrium from Quantum-Field Entanglement
item.description: arXiv:2609.33188v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Entanglement harvesting allows localized probes to extract entanglement from a quantum field, even when their interaction regions are spacelike separated. However, how the resource obtained by the probes can be operationalized remains largely open. In this work, we ask whether the harvested entanglement can influence the timing choices of observers acting as players. We construct a quantum input game for Alice and Bob, each controlling an Unruh-DeWitt detector that couples to the vacuum of a free massless scalar field in four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime. Each player can choose an early interaction time, a late interaction time, or exit. After joint entry, a referee sends independent question qubits, so that fixed local Bell measurements and a payment table convert the detector state into a payoff. The mean payoff is proportional to minus the expectation value of an entanglement witness and is nonpositive for every separable resource. We calculate the detector state to leading perturbative order and solve the participation game analytically. Away from payoff degeneracies, every timing equilibrium with positive payoff gives two trembling hand perfect participation equilibria, in addition to mutual exit. The total count can therefore be one, three, five, or seven. For one fixed switching function and timing menu, five selected delays give the sequence seven, three, one, seven, and one. The timing payoffs follow from the field's two-point functions, with the Hadamard and Pauli-Jordan contributions to the coherence competing against local excitation noise. The resulting equilibrium structure provides an operational setting for studying how vacuum correlations and causal propagation affect the strategic use of quantum-field entanglement.
item.dc:creator: Hao Xu

item.title: Quantum Complexity of Ancilla-Free Unitary Embeddings for Nonlinear Dynamics via Generalized State-Dependent Double-Bracket Flows
item.description: arXiv:2609.37802v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulating nonlinear dynamics with quantum computers has gained increasing attention. In general, such simulations require additional quantum resources because unitary quantum evolution is linear. A fundamental question is how nonlinear dynamics can be embedded into fully coherent, ancilla-free unitary circuits and how the complexity of the dynamics governs the required quantum resources. In this work, we generalize the ancilla-free double-bracket quantum algorithm for imaginary-time evolution by replacing its state-independent Hamiltonian with a state-dependent Hermitian operator. Our framework recursively calls an initial state preparation oracle and its inverse, and prepares the target solution to any prescribed accuracy using a fully coherent, ancilla-free unitary embedding. We relate the query cost to the complexity of the nonlinear dynamics, specifically their sensitivity to initial conditions. We obtain query upper bounds of $\exp(O(T))$, $\exp(O(T^2))$, and $\exp(\exp(O(T)))$ when the distance between solutions contracts at least exponentially (contractive), does not increase (nonexpansive), or grows at most exponentially (expansive), respectively, where $T$ is the target evolution time. For the discrete Gross--Pitaevskii equation, our ancilla-free double-bracket circuit achieves optimal worst-case query complexity $\Theta(e^{gT/2})$ over a specified family of single-qubit initial states, where $g>0$ is the nonlinearity strength. These results connect the complexity of nonlinear dynamics to the query cost of coherent quantum simulation and provide a foundation for designing ancilla-free unitary embeddings with optimal query complexity.
item.dc:creator: Yuki Ito, Hideaki Hakoshima, Keisuke Fujii

item.title: Local Automorphism-Aware Syndrome Compilation for General Quantum LDPC Codes
item.description: arXiv:2609.40319v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Low-depth syndrome extraction for Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) quantum low-density parity-check codes can be formulated as a proper ordered edge-coloring problem subject to quantum parity constraints. A proper edge-coloring of the CSS Tanner graph ensures that each data or ancilla qubit participates in at most one two-qubit gate per layer, but does not guarantee a valid interleaving of the X- and Z-check measurements as for every overlapping X/Z check pair, the number of shared data qubits on which the X interaction precedes the Z interaction must be even. The minimum number of colors in a proper ordered edge-coloring satisfying the quantum parity constraints equals the minimum two-qubit depth when each stabilizer check is measured with a single ancilla. We introduce local automorphism-aware syndrome compilation (LocalASC), which reduces the constraint system to edge-orbit variables under a subgroup of the Tanner graph automorphisms and lifts each feasible orbit assignment to the full graph. Although the $6$-layer degree lower bound is unattainable for the published weight-$6$ IBM bivariate bicycle codes, we show that this is not universal among two-block CSS codes. Among code instances for which the maximum check weight equals the maximum Tanner graph degree, LocalASC finds depth-optimal syndrome-extraction schedules for several two-block CSS codes with odd component weights, including instances with unequal odd weights. We also obtain lower-bound-saturating syndrome-extraction schedules for several quantum Tanner codes satisfying the same degree condition. To obtain the subgroups used by LocalASC without computing the full automorphism group of the Tanner graph, we construct translation subgroups for two-block group-algebra CSS codes over abelian groups. For quantum Tanner codes, we give conditions under which square-complex symmetries extend to Tanner graph automorphisms.
item.dc:creator: Eugenio Durazo Rocha, Olai \AA. Mostad, Hsuan-Yin Lin, Eirik Rosnes

item.title: Sparse Hamiltonian simulation with optimal dependence on the maximum column Euclidean norm
item.description: arXiv:2610.02030v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a quantum algorithm for simulating a $d$-sparse Hermitian Hamiltonian $H$, assuming known upper bounds $\Lambda$ on its maximum column Euclidean norm $\|H\|_{1\to2}$ and $\Lambda_{\max}$ on its maximum entry magnitude. For every $t\ge0$, simulation with operator-norm error $\epsilon$ uses \[ O\!\left(t\Lambda\sqrt d +\sqrt{td\Lambda_{\max}\log(2/\epsilon)}+\log(2/\epsilon)\right) \] sparse-oracle queries. This removes the subpolynomial overhead in Low's algorithm [STOC 2019]. For $d>1$ and $t\Lambda\ge\log(2/\epsilon)$, the bound matches the worst-case lower bound. A known spectral-norm upper bound may also be used in place of $\Lambda$. The number of 1- and 2-qubit gates is linear in the query scale, up to oracle costs and polynomial overhead in the input bit lengths and logarithmic precision parameters. As applications, we obtain $O(\kappa\sqrt d\,\mathrm{polylog}(\kappa/\epsilon))$ queries for solving $d$-sparse quantum linear systems with $\|A\|\le1$ and $\|A^{-1}\|\le\kappa$, under standard sparse and state-preparation access. We also give a gate-efficient implementation of black-box unitaries with at most $d$ nonzero entries per row and column using $O(\sqrt{d\log(2/\epsilon)}+\log(2/\epsilon))$ queries, given sparse access to the unitary and its adjoint. At constant error, the query bound is optimal and yields $\Theta(\sqrt N)$ queries for arbitrary $N\times N$ unitaries, resolving the open question on black-box unitary implementation posed by Berry and Childs [QIC 2012].
item.dc:creator: Zecheng Li, Chunhao Wang

item.title: Root-sparsity scaling for Hamiltonian simulation, differential equations and linear-system solvers
item.description: arXiv:2610.02939v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give quantum algorithms for time-independent and time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation, linear differential equations and linear systems, all with complexity that has only square-root dependence on matrix sparsity. Our algorithms retain optimal scaling in other relevant parameters such as time, condition number and precision. For several cases we prove matching lower bounds on the joint parameters and show that the additional gate overhead is only polylogarithmic in the inverse precision. The common primitive connecting our algorithms is the Cayley transform, which provides a cheap unitary embedding of the sparse matrices. For Hamiltonian simulation and differential equations, we then use transducers to construct the desired evolution operators. For linear systems, we instead encode the solution in the kernel of a matrix and use the Cayley transform to construct a projector onto that kernel.
item.dc:creator: Dominic W. Berry, Abhishek Rawat, Sophia Simon, Guang Hao Low

item.title: The Mermin-Peres Magic Square Game With Three or More Players
item.description: arXiv:2610.06534v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a generalization of the Mermin-Peres magic square game to $N$ players, in which the square is replaced by an $N$-dimensional hypercube. We show that the winning probability of the optimal classical strategy remains $8/9$ for all $N$, while for $N \ge 3$, a generalization of the quantum strategy for $N = 2$ achieves a winning probability between $1/3$ and $3/4$. This loss of quantum advantage for $N \ge 3$ is a consequence of monogamy.
item.dc:creator: Itamar Lorian, J. E. Avron

item.title: The parliament of observers - Against the observable axiom of quantum mechanics
item.description: arXiv:2610.07254v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The 'unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences' may at times give the impression that natural science, especially modern theoretical physics, is all but a formal apparatus. However, a key challenge of physics remains to align everyday notions of experience -- be it directly or mediated through instruments of arbitrary sophistication -- with their mathematical formalisation. This applies in particular to quantum theory, arguably the most successful theory of physics ever invented. One of its core assumptions postulates: $(Sharp)\ observables\ correspond\ with\ self-adjoint\ operators.$ Here, we argue that already this most basic premise about the quantum formalism falls apart under careful scrutiny, at least when understood for all observables at once. In other words, we challenge the role of the noncommutative algebra of bounded operators as an adequate formalisation of the 'algebra of observables', understood as (equivalence classes of) measurement procedures that admit a coherent empirical interpretation.
item.dc:creator: Markus Frembs, Andreas D\"oring

item.title: No-Disturbance-without-Uncertainty generates the Quantum set in the simplest Bell scenario
item.description: arXiv:2610.08749v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Characterizing the set of quantum nonlocal correlations through information-theoretic constraints is a central problem in quantum foundations. We show that the convex hull of no-signalling behaviors in a bipartite Bell experiment satisfying a common-overlap no-disturbance-without-uncertainty condition is exactly the finite-dimensional quantum set whenever one party has two binary measurements and the other has an arbitrary finite number of settings, each with an arbitrary finite number of outcomes. In the simplest binary input-output Bell scenario, this characterizes the full eight-dimensional set of quantum behaviors, including the local marginals. The proof constructs a quantum realization directly from the conditional probabilities and no-signalling. The characterization also reduces optimization of any linear Bell expression in these scenarios to maximization over a one-parameter family of second-order cone programs. The results establish a connection between local uncertainty-disturbance constraints and quantum nonlocality, mediated by no-signalling and shared classical randomness.
item.dc:creator: Ravishankar Ramanathan

item.title: Extensively degenerate superradiant phase in a giant-atom quantum Rabi ring
item.description: arXiv:2610.09880v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that an $N$-site quantum Rabi ring with matched giant-atom couplings has $2^N$ degenerate superradiant configurations as the atomic-to-cavity frequency ratio $\eta=\Delta/\omega$ tends to infinity. Each atom couples to two cavities separated by two lattice spacings, and the photon hopping carries a phase $\pi/2$. Matching the ratio of the two coupling strengths to the dimensionless photon hopping reduces the mean-field energy to a sum of single-site Rabi energies, with a common critical coupling for all momentum-pair sectors. The degeneracy survives quadratic quantum fluctuations despite a dispersive excitation spectrum. At large but finite $\eta$, second-order processes involving the local cubic anharmonicity generate a same-sublattice Ising coupling of order $\omega/\eta$, selecting ferro- and antiferro-superradiant configurations. This quantum order-by-disorder effect has no classical counterpart. Four-site calculations retaining all spin states quantitatively support the predicted energy coefficients. The separation between the induced coupling and the excitation gap allows a broad temperature interval with macroscopic photon occupation and short-range correlations between displacement signs.
item.dc:creator: Shu He, Li-Wei Duan

item.title: Sample-Based Quantum Krylov Galerkin Solvers for Elliptic Partial Differential Equations on Curved Geometries with Hardware Validation
item.description: arXiv:2610.15586v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sample-based quantum solvers measure time-evolved Krylov states and solve the problem classically on the observed basis states. We develop this approach for the positive-definite linear systems of elliptic partial differential equations. A Galerkin solve on the sampled Fourier modes gives the solution. We derive energy-norm error bounds that connect the measured outcome law to the solution error, a sample complexity, and a support-completeness theorem. The theorem shows that time averaging recovers solution modes that are hidden from every selection based on the source. For curved cross sections we give a constructive procedure: conformal coordinates fix the matrix class, isometries of the cross section give postselection rules that keep every solution mode, and the Lie derivative of the metric bounds the error from geometric uncertainty. We apply the method to pulsatile flow in elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts and to non-separable problems with up to 16 qubits. On 16 qubits the sampler reaches 0.2% error with 3% of the Fourier modes, while a selection from the source stalls at 13% error. At these sizes a classical residual-greedy selection is more accurate, but its cost grows with the full dimension, whereas the sampler and the reduced Galerkin solve scale with the number of sampled modes. On IonQ and IBM processors with six and eight qubits, the measured outcome laws follow a replacement-noise model with a common decay of about 0.6% per two-qubit gate, and a parity rule derived from the geometry detects noisy shots at the predicted rate.
item.dc:creator: Doyeol "David" Ahn (Center for Quantum Information Processing, University of Seoul, Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea, Singularity Quantum Inc., Villa Park, California, USA), Byeongyong Park (Center for Quantum Information Processing, University of Seoul, Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul, Republic of Korea)

item.title: Time-Frequency Continuous-Variable Quantum Teleportation with Single Photons
item.description: arXiv:2610.16198v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum teleportation, a key building block for quantum technologies, enables distant parties, Alice and Bob, to transfer an unknown quantum state using entanglement, local operations, and classical communication. In this work, we propose a quantum teleportation protocol for single-photon time-frequency continuous variables, where time is the time of arrival at a detector. We detail the operational requirements of the protocol, notably the nonlinear interactions needed for the photon-photon time-frequency entangling gate. By explicitly treating the detector position as the reference frame for time of arrival, we show that, even with ideal classical and quantum channels, the input-output fidelity is not unity unless the receiving party can correct the detector-position mismatch. This results in a trade-off between teleportation fidelity and the temporal bandwidth of the input photon wavepacket. The protocol itself can be used for remote detector synchronization. In particular, we show that time-frequency cat and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states provide an internal temporal ruler through fidelity revivals. We further derive the classical and best-copy fidelity thresholds for single-photon Gaussian wavepackets, finding that the relevant vacuum-equivalent shot noise is input-dependent, in contrast with quadrature-based continuous-variable quantum teleportation. Our proposal derives from a quantum theory of space-time events, whereafter we establish space as a reference for the time degree of freedom, thereby grounding our work in ongoing research on reference frames and superselection rules in quantum optics and quantum information. Beyond protocols harnessing time-frequency continuous variables of single photons, this work points toward remote synchronization in quantum communication architectures.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Meguebel, Nadia Belabas, Nicolas Fabre

item.title: Geodesic steering for rapid dissipative entanglement distribution
item.description: arXiv:2610.16854v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe an optimal-control strategy designed to accelerate the dissipative preparation of complex, highly entangled quantum many-body states. Analogous to optimal steering of isolated quantum systems, our scheme identifies control pulses that guide the evolution of open quantum systems along trajectories of instantaneous steady states while minimizing leakage resulting from non-adiabatic transitions. In many cases of interest, these control parameters can be derived analytically and without the need for computationally expensive numerical simulations of the full many-body master equation. We apply this technique for the preparation of bi- and multipartite entangled states in qubit systems coupled to a common photonic waveguide or a distributed squeezed reservoir. In both scenarios, our optimal-control strategy significantly outperforms the bare relaxation dynamics after a quench, reducing preparation times of near-maximally entangled states by orders of magnitude. This drastic speedup makes dissipative entanglement distribution protocols compatible with high-fidelity quantum information processing applications and illustrates more broadly the potential of leakage minimization for accelerating reservoir-engineering schemes.
item.dc:creator: Keshav Venkataraman, Pablo Martinez-Azcona, Marko Ljubotina, Adrian Parra-Rodriguez, Peter Rabl

item.title: Under what conditions can coupling disorder render qubit dynamics CP-divisible in a finite spin bath?
item.description: arXiv:2610.18582v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate whether unresolved quasi-static Gaussian disorder in system--bath coupling can make finite spin-bath dynamics CP-divisible. The coupling varies between shots but is fixed within each, yielding a disorder-averaged tomographic map. For a single-spin Ising $ZZ$ bath with a fixed initial state, disorder can induce a polarization-dependent transition to CP-divisibility. A bath fully polarized along the longitudinal direction ($|m_z|=1$) yields CP-divisible dynamics irrespective of disorder, whereas zero longitudinal polarization or Haar-sampled bath states fluctuating independently of the coupling between shots preserve CP-indivisibility at any finite disorder strength for nonzero mean coupling. We extend this analytically to inhomogeneous Ising baths of any finite size $N$. For factorized bath preparations, one spin with zero longitudinal polarization and nonzero mean coupling suffices to retain CP-indivisibility at finite disorder. Strong disorder can render partially polarized baths CP-divisible. For homogeneous baths, the critical disorder ratio is independent of $N$. When bath states fluctuate physically between shots, independent Haar sampling preserves CP-indivisibility for finite $N$ if any mean coupling is nonzero. For a single-spin anisotropic Heisenberg bath, any nonzero transverse exchange preserves trace-distance backflow at finite disorder for every fixed preparation, provided the mean coupling is nonzero. Exact diagonalization up to $N=12$ shows trace-distance revivals for a fully polarized bath, in Haar averages over fixed product bath states, and for fluctuating bath states. Transverse exchange and physical bath-state fluctuations with zero average longitudinal polarization preserve CP-indivisibility at finite disorder. Yet increasing disorder can make trace-distance revivals experimentally unresolvable, making the dynamics appear Markovian.
item.dc:creator: Sayan Sengupta, Anish Sharma, George Biswas, Anindya Biswas

item.title: Shot- and Noise-Aware Pauli Correlation Encoding for Max-Cut Experiments on IBM Heron Quantum Processor
item.description: arXiv:2610.19544v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pauli correlation encoding (PCE) encodes $m$ binary variables in the signs of $k$-body Pauli correlators of $n=O(m^{1/k})$ qubits, and trains a parameterized circuit on a relaxed loss of sharpness $\alpha$. The strongest published schedules sharpen this loss aggressively and are benchmarked with exact expectation values, whereas a quantum computer estimates correlators from a finite number of shots. We show that the sharpness is a hidden shot budget. Since the expected sign of a correlator estimated from $S$ shots, $\mathrm{erf}(c\sqrt{S/2})$, agrees with $\tanh(0.851\sqrt{S}\,c)$ to within $0.019$, the edge term of the relaxed loss at $\alpha=0.851\sqrt{S}$ approximately equals, up to a constant, minus twice the cut expected from decoding $S$ shots. This explains why schedules tuned with exact expectation values lose their advantage at realistic budgets, and yields a shot-aware schedule whose final sharpness is set by the shot budget. On five G-set graphs with $800$ variables on $13$ qubits, this schedule outperforms every published schedule at its target budget in all $150$ paired comparisons of the decoded circuit output, owing to the sharpness at $1.6\times10^4$ shots and mostly to switching off the regularization at $10^3$; after a classical bit-swap search, it remains the best on average at $1.6\times10^4$ shots. Device noise damps the correlators by a factor $s$, which amounts to a smaller shot budget $s^2S$. On the IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, an all-to-all ansatz of the type used for the best published G-set results compiles to $835$ CZ gates and decodes to a random cut, while our $96$-CZ hardware-native circuit, trained in simulation and sharpened to $\alpha\simeq0.65\,s\sqrt{S}$, retains up to $0.919$ of the best-known cut. For new circuits, a damping and an offset calibrated on other circuits of the same graph predicted the decoded cuts at $10^3$ shots to within $0.002$.
item.dc:creator: Achraf Boussahi

item.title: Strong subadditivity of topological entropy on the torus: R\'enyi order and non-Abelian structure
item.description: arXiv:2610.20078v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We classify universal strong subadditivity of the canonical topological entropy on an unpunctured torus across all pure logical states and admissible region pairs, for finite unitary modular tensor categories and finite positive R\'enyi orders. Below order one, universal validity is equivalent to Abelian, or pointed, anyon structure. At the von Neumann order it holds for every category. In nonpointed categories, shared topological flux and unequal occupied quantum dimensions curve the multi-annulus response, producing violations at every finite positive order other than one. Every category of rank greater than one admits a single state and region pair that violate the inequality for all finite orders at least two. The remaining pointed orders strictly between one and two are governed by an exact equal-order modular Fourier criterion. On the lattice, a specified quantum-double reference ground state for each finite non-Abelian group realizes the nonpointed violations directly in ordinary physical-edge entropies on a common refinement. Applying the same diagonal filter to every physical edge gives a controlled deformation of this reference state. For each fixed group, a common size-independent small parameter interval supports a uniform R\'enyi-two deficit bound and a uniformly gapped local parent for all cost profiles bounded between zero and one, within the stated lattice family. Nonconstant profiles change regional entanglement spectra near the fixed point at every fixed finite volume in the specified strip geometry. The deficit converges to its strictly negative fixed-point value in the controlled joint limit of system size and interface separation.
item.dc:creator: Yi Liang

item.title: Trial-space co-design for quantum simulation on noisy hardware
item.description: arXiv:2610.33246v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum simulations on noisy hardware are often designed as if the machine were ideal, with device limitations considered only after the basis and measurement plan have been chosen. We instead use information about the physical problem and the device at an earlier stage, to decide which states and evolution times should form a compact simulation basis. Because the target problem remains unchanged, the method adapts only the representation used to solve it. Tests on many-body and molecular models show that this approach can reveal useful directions that ordinary time evolution misses, while also exposing an important limitation: some of these directions can become too similar to estimate reliably. Realistic device data further show that hardware response can change the preferred states and evolution times before execution. Across seven acquisition days, a four-qubit experiment shows a median 54\% reduction in projected-energy error from problem-informed time choices relative to uniform sampling under matched hardware conditions. These results provide a proof of principle for simulation-basis design as a practical interface between quantum algorithms and the hardware that executes them.
item.dc:creator: Bo Peng, Vibin Abraham, Himadri Pathak

item.title: Fast and accurate rare-event simulation by Markov chain Monte Carlo for general quantum codes
item.description: arXiv:2610.35498v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The splitting method estimates logical error rates of quantum error-correcting codes deep in the rare-event regime, where direct Monte Carlo sampling is prohibitively expensive. It relies on a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler of faulty configurations, usually driven by one-bit-flip proposals. However, one-bit flips have been reported to be trapped on some codes, which biases the estimate. To address this issue, we propose a new kernel that combines locally balanced one-bit-flip proposals with a cluster-exchange move. We benchmark both kernels and direct Monte Carlo on twelve codes under code-capacity bit-flip noise in two ways, by comparing the mean fault weight with an MCMC-independent reference and by measuring the computation time to reach a fixed accuracy. In the first, our kernel agrees with the reference on every code, including those where one-bit flips are trapped. In the second, it is faster than one-bit flips wherever they are trapped, by orders of magnitude on some codes. Furthermore, at the lowest error rate, it is faster than direct Monte Carlo on every code, by more than four orders of magnitude on some.
item.dc:creator: Junichi Haruna, Kotaro Murakami

item.title: Diagnostic-dependent lasting Mpemba effect in a parametrically driven oscillator
item.description: arXiv:2610.36663v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agreement on the initial order does not ensure agreement on the late-time behavior in the quantum Mpemba effect. For a pair of centered Gaussian preparations of a detuned parametric oscillator below threshold, three diagnostics initially give the same order. At late times, the trace distance shows a lasting Mpemba reversal, the relative entropy recovers the initial order, and the Hilbert-Schmidt distances cross at arbitrarily late times. An asymptotic analysis establishes these behaviors and their stability under small changes of the initial covariances and the quadratic generator. Equal decay rates keep an energy mode and a pair of squeezing modes comparable at late times. This structure holds for stable single-mode quadratic generators with linear damping in the elliptic regime. The diagnostics weight the resulting purity and squeezing deviations differently; near a pure stationary state, the relative entropy is particularly sensitive to purity deviations. Weak perturbations can split these rates and select a dominant branch. For the same pair, number dephasing restores the initial order in all three diagnostics, possibly only after the signal falls below measurement resolution. A Kerr perturbation selecting the squeezing pair instead produces a common lasting reversal.
item.dc:creator: Shu He

item.title: Maximum-Entropy Ensemble of Quantum Subsystems with a Fixed Average State
item.description: arXiv:2610.39712v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The reduced density matrices of Haar-random bipartite states form a fixed-trace version of the Wishart ensemble of random matrices, with an asymptotic eigenvalue density given by the Marchenko-Pastur (MP) law. We establish a similar universal form for the maximum-entropy distribution of mixed states subject to a fixed ensemble average, arguing that its eigenvalue density converges asymptotically to that of the correlated Wishart ensemble (CWE). The density is thus obtained by a free multiplicative convolution formula, which we apply to the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) with a thermal average state to derive a high-temperature leading-order correction to the MP law. We then consider measurement by a random POVM on the purification of the mixed reference state. We show that the resulting mixed-state ensemble is asymptotically equivalent to the CWE, and provide confirming numerical evidence. We return to the TFIM example to compute the entanglement of the system with the ancilla after measurement, and give finite-temperature Page curves for the average entanglement entropies.
item.dc:creator: Charlie Shakeshaft, Christopher David White, Harry J. D. Miller

item.title: Comment on "Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings" (arXiv:2610.26833)
item.description: arXiv:2611.05105v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We discuss the relationship between quantum Hamiltonian embeddings (arXiv:2610.26833) and prior developments in Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML), including QCML's earlier implementation on IBM quantum hardware. We examine the novelty claims and the computational role of encoding the training data in a shared ground state. We assess the scope of the trainability and generalization guarantees and identify missing comparisons with relevant classical alternatives. For the reported experimental model, whose inference is entirely classical, the paper does not establish a computational advantage for quantum training.
item.dc:creator: Alexander G. Abanov, Luca Candelori, Kharen Musaelian

item.title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
item.description: arXiv:2611.05355v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every nonlinearity is a quadratic detection - an interference, a balanced reading or a camera - and the output is a Born probability: attention |<q|k>|^2, the form of the Born rule, normalised per row, a measured product for the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout; between detections, classical control rescales and re-encodes. With its denominators held at the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share to 10^-13. On e-SNLI natural language inference it reaches 77.45 +- 0.91 % accuracy, level with a same-size softmax transformer (76.62 +- 0.36 %) and an order-free bag of embeddings (77.79 %). Exactness buys the sum, not the best ranking. Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 44 % of pairs, of the 53 % some deletion changes, against 31-32 % for the softmax model's integrated gradients; the model's own gradient x input does as well (43 %), as does a bag of embeddings' (43 %, seed 0), and leave-one-out does better. Holding the denominators helps the low end: the five words ranked last change the answer in 1 %, against 6 % free. The same weights compile exactly to simulated optoelectronics, and their attention to qubits. On ibm_kingston, reading only the attention, the device gave the model's answers in all three Hadamard-test runs (the two shortest pairs and one without its deciding word) and both compute-uncompute runs (one circuit per overlap); uniform attention answers otherwise on two of the three inputs. With the device's row sums the evidence correlated with the exact one at 0.997 and 0.962 by Hadamard tests; with compute-uncompute, 0.971 and 0.48.
item.dc:creator: Teerawat Tongloy, Jiraporn Pongsopa, Rangsan Jomtarak

item.title: Certifying the Rydberg-exposure limit of a globally driven controlled-Z gate
item.description: arXiv:2611.07388v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rydberg excitation enables entangling gates in neutral-atom quantum processors but also exposes them to spontaneous decay. Whether this exposure can be made arbitrarily small through pulse shaping and longer gate times has remained unresolved. We show that an exact controlled-$Z$ gate driven by a single global laser has an irreducible Rydberg-exposure cost in the perfect-blockade regime. The product of the maximum Rabi frequency $\Omega_{\max}$ and the average time $T_R$ spent in the Rydberg state is bounded below by $2.9312$, independent of pulse shape and duration. We derive this bound using a sum-of-squares certificate, strengthened by constraints imposed by the shared drive. Using interval arithmetic, we also certify the existence of an exact gate pulse with $\Omega_{max} T_R<2.9359$. The unrounded bounds differ by less than $0.16\%$. The bound identifies a fundamental cost of shared-drive entangling dynamics and establishes a benchmark against which future gate-control strategies can be assessed.
item.dc:creator: Yusheng Zhao, Han Wang, Mingrui Jing, Zhongyi Ni, Hongshun Yao, Xin Wang, Jie Wang, Jinguo Liu

item.title: Accelerating Quantum-Classical Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo with Shadow-Trained Neural Quantum States
item.description: arXiv:2611.08129v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum-classical auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (QC-AFQMC) uses a trial state prepared on a quantum computer to improve the accuracy of the classical AFQMC algorithm. State-of-the-art QC-AFQMC represents this state with matchgate shadows, so every trial-walker overlap and local energy must be averaged over many snapshots, making this classical computation a bottleneck. Here we distill the matchgate shadow data into a symmetry-constrained, noise-aware, autoregressive transformer neural quantum state (NQS). Used as the AFQMC trial state, the NQS evaluates overlaps, force biases, and local energies without repeatedly summing over the matchgate shadows. For a nickel-catalyzed oxidative-addition reaction, the noise-awareness of our NQS design successfully recovers the ideal-upCCD AFQMC barrier and reaction energy within statistical uncertainty, while standard QC-AFQMC execution with the same shadow data yields qualitatively inaccurate results as a result of hardware noise. Since the shadow data are needed only for training, the estimated classical cost for the nickel system falls by approximately 99% relative to our previous QC-AFQMC implementation.
item.dc:creator: Justin Provazza, Oliver Knitter, Joshua Goings, Evgeny Epifanovsky, Chi Chen, Martin Roetteler, Luning Zhao

item.title: Model-family selection and recovery-gate design in generator-based noise tomography
